title: “JUDGE NOT” — THE BIBLE VERSE ALMOST EVERYONE MISUNDERSTANDS
paragraphs:
“JUDGE NOT” — THE BIBLE VERSE ALMOST EVERYONE MISUNDERSTANDS
Jesus Never Said, “Never Call Sin Sin.” What He Actually Said Is Far More Uncomfortable.
Maybe someone has said it to you.
Maybe you were trying to warn someone you loved about a road that was slowly destroying them, and before you could finish the sentence, those three words came back like a slammed door:
And yet there is a frightening possibility most people never consider:
What if one of the most quoted statements of Jesus has become one of the most misunderstood?
What if “Judge not” does not mean what our culture often makes it mean?
And what if Jesus was not giving humanity permission to stop distinguishing truth from error, holiness from sin, or good fruit from poisonous fruit?
“Judge not, that ye be not judged.”
They are not ours to soften, erase, or explain away.
But neither are they ours to rip from the mouth of Christ and make them say something Christ Himself did not mean.
“Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.”
The word translated “judge” comes from κρίνω — krinō, a word whose meaning depends upon context. It can refer to judging, deciding, evaluating, passing judgment, or condemning.
Because if Matthew 7:1 means that Christians must never make any moral evaluation whatsoever, Jesus appears to contradict Himself only a few sentences later.
“Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine…”
How could anyone obey that instruction without making some kind of discernment?
“Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.”
But how do you recognize a false prophet if you are forbidden from evaluating anyone?
“Ye shall know them by their fruits.”
And elsewhere Jesus says something even more explicit:
“Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.”
μὴ κρίνετε κατ’ ὄψιν, ἀλλὰ τὴν δικαίαν κρίσιν κρίνατε.
Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment.
So Jesus cannot possibly mean, “Never discern. Never evaluate. Never recognize sin. Never distinguish truth from deception.”
Something deeper is happening in Matthew 7.
And once you see it, “Judge not” stops being a weapon you can comfortably point at somebody else.
“For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.”
Then comes the picture that should make every self-righteous heart uncomfortable.
“And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?”
A man walks toward his brother.
He is deeply concerned about the tiny speck.
Except there is a massive beam sticking out of his own face.
He keeps turning his head and knocking things over while trying to perform delicate eye surgery on somebody else.
Until Jesus gives him a name.
That is the wound beneath the verse.
The terrifying human ability to become intensely aware of somebody else’s sin while becoming strangely blind to our own.
Not the character assassination disguised as “concern” coming from our own mouth.
And somehow, while examining everybody else under a spiritual microscope, we manage to keep ourselves conveniently out of focus.
He does not finish by saying:
“Therefore leave the speck in your brother’s eye.”
“First cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother’s eye.”
Jesus does not abolish loving correction.
He purifies the person doing it.
Then, if necessary, approach your brother.
Christian correction was never supposed to sound like:
“I know what it is to need mercy too. There is something hurting you, and I love you too much to pretend it isn’t there.”
That is radically different from condemnation.
And Scripture refuses to let Christians hide behind a counterfeit version of “Judge not.”
Jesus Himself teaches in Matthew 18 that when a brother sins, there are circumstances in which the believer should go to him privately and address the matter.
“Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness…”
“…considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.”
There is Matthew 7 again in another form.
Look at yourself while helping someone else.
Remember your weakness while confronting theirs.
Never forget that the person correcting the sinner is also a sinner who survives entirely by grace.

The New Testament even commands church discipline in serious circumstances. Paul addresses blatant, unrepentant sin within the church in 1 Corinthians 5. Jesus gives instructions concerning escalating correction in Matthew 18:15–17.
So biblical love cannot mean moral silence.
But biblical truth also cannot mean merciless condemnation.
We have somehow become experts at choosing one ditch or the other.
“Truth gives me permission to crush you.”
Jesus stands between them with wounds in His hands.
Look at the woman caught in adultery in John 8.
She is dragged into public view.
Men stand around her carrying stones.
Imagine knowing that strangers are discussing your worst moment while you stand exposed in the middle of them.
“He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.”
And eventually she is standing before the only Man present who truly is without sin.
The One who actually possesses the moral authority everyone else was pretending to possess.
But He does not stop there.
Jesus does not call adultery righteousness.
He does not say holiness no longer matters.
But neither does He destroy the sinner standing before Him.
That is the Gospel in miniature.
And perhaps that is exactly why this teaching hurts so deeply.
Because some of us have been the woman.
And some of us have been holding the stone.
Some of us have been both.
Maybe you know what it feels like to have your worst season become somebody else’s favorite story about you.
Maybe people still remember the version of you that Jesus has been changing.
The thing you wish you could erase.
And whenever you walk into certain rooms, you can almost feel your history arriving before you do.
But they do not know what happened when you finally collapsed before Jesus.
They do not know how many nights you cried.
They do not know where Christ found you.
God remembers the moment you finally reached toward the One who could break them.
This is where Christianity becomes unlike every human courtroom.
The Gospel does not say sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more than we ever imagined.
But the cross also proves that mercy runs deeper than we ever deserved.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
And yet Romans continues by pointing us toward justification through God’s grace and the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
At the cross, we discover something devastating:
He did not rescue us because our record was clean.
Christ “died for our sins according to the scriptures” and rose again, as Paul proclaims in 1 Corinthians 15.
Not sinners pretending to be judges over other sinners.
Not sinners pretending sin is harmless.
Sinners pointing other sinners toward the Savior.
So before you expose someone, ask whether you have examined yourself.
Before you post about them, ask whether restoration or humiliation is your goal.
Before you repeat the story, ask whether you would want Christ to broadcast every detail of yours.
Before you speak truth, remove the beam.
And if correction really is necessary, go carrying a towel instead of a trophy.
Go like someone who knows Calvary.
Go like someone who understands that you are not the Savior in the conversation.
Your job is not to win the courtroom.
Your desire should be to win your brother.
And if you are the person being corrected, do not automatically use “Judge not” as armor against every uncomfortable truth.
Sometimes the person willing to risk your anger by telling you the truth loves you more than the people applauding while you destroy yourself.
“Faithful are the wounds of a friend…”
Not every wound is an attack.
Sometimes God loves us enough to interrupt us.
The question is whether the correction agrees with Scripture and whether we are humble enough to examine ourselves before God.
And there is another side Christians desperately need to recover.
Someone’s past sin does not give you permanent ownership of their identity.
If Christ has forgiven them, who are you to keep resurrecting what Jesus died to redeem?
The Gospel is filled with people whose worst chapters did not become their final chapters.
Imagine looking into the eyes of the Savior after insisting you never knew Him.
Peter’s story could have ended around a charcoal fire with denial hanging in the air.
Later, beside another charcoal fire, Jesus restored him.
Failure did not receive the final sentence.
Then grace met him on the Damascus road.
The persecutor became the apostle who proclaimed the Christ he once opposed.
That does not minimize what Saul did.
It magnifies what Jesus can do.
This is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to one truth:
But because when Jesus Christ saves a person, sin no longer possesses the authority to write the ending.
Maybe everybody else keeps calling you by the chapter Jesus already turned.
Maybe your mind still introduces you by your failure.
But if you are in Christ, Scripture gives you another word.
Not because you became perfect overnight.
Because your righteousness is found in Christ.
That should destroy both pride and despair.
You cannot look down on another sinner because you were rescued by grace.
And you do not have to remain crushed beneath your own condemnation because Jesus paid for sinners with His blood.
The cross leaves nobody room to boast.
And it leaves repentant sinners enormous room to hope.
So what does “Judge not” actually demand from us?
Something much harder than simply never having an opinion about right and wrong.
Jesus calls us to become people whose discernment has been washed in humility.
People who can call sin sin without forgetting they need grace.
People who can confront without enjoying condemnation.
People who can forgive because they remember how much they have been forgiven.
People who care more about restoration than reputation.
People who refuse both self-righteousness and moral cowardice.
People who look into their own eyes before reaching toward the speck in somebody else’s.
And perhaps right now the Holy Spirit is not bringing somebody else to your mind.
Perhaps He is bringing you to your mind.
The private compromise nobody at church knows about.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you out of the darkness that is killing you.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is a cross strong enough for what you have done.
There is an empty tomb powerful enough for what you have become.
Not cheap grace that tells you to stay chained.
Saving grace that breaks chains and teaches you to walk with Christ.
So maybe today you need to stop throwing stones.
Maybe you need to stop hiding behind “Judge not.”
Maybe you need to forgive someone Christ has been rebuilding.
Maybe you need to receive correction instead of immediately becoming defensive.
Maybe you need to come home.
Whatever brought you here, do not leave with merely a better interpretation of Matthew 7.
Leave with a clearer view of Jesus.
The One who tells hypocrites to put down their stones.
The One who tells sinners to leave their sin.
The One who receives repentant people.
The One who bore judgment at Calvary so guilty people could receive mercy through faith in Him.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to explain your whole story publicly. But you can take one honest step.
Supporting Gospel-centered work can itself be one practical way to glorify God when it is done freely, prayerfully, and from a heart that desires to help biblical truth reach more people.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about becoming better at identifying everybody else’s stains.
It is about realizing that we could never wash away our own.
And then discovering that Jesus Christ came for sinners.
And He still receives people who come to Him in repentance and faith.
So the next time you hear someone say, “Judge not,” remember the beam.
Remember the stones dropping from human hands.
Remember the woman standing before Jesus.
Because maybe the person you were preparing to condemn is standing one chapter away from a testimony you cannot yet see.
And maybe the scandal you thought would become the title of your life is only the chapter where Jesus begins rewriting the ending.
The hands that have every right to condemn the repentant sinner are the very hands that were pierced to save them.
